text: Somewhere at the bottom of the Pacific Ocean, there's a stone wheel taller than a man. It sank more than a hundred years ago. Nobody could reach it. And yet, for generations, it made one family rich. Not rich in a story. Rich in real life. They could spend it. Everyone on the island agreed it still counted. So here's a strange question. If a fortune can sit where nobody can touch it, and still work, then what is money, really? By the end of this video, you'll see that the money in your bank account works exactly like that stone. And you'll learn the one thing money can never, ever buy more of.

This is Yap. A small group of islands in the western Pacific. For centuries, the people here used a kind of money unlike anything else on Earth. Giant wheels of stone, called rai. Some were small enough to hold in your hand. The biggest were twelve feet across and heavier than a car. And here's the wild part. There's no stone like this on Yap. Every one was carved on another island, Palau, about two hundred and fifty miles away. Men sailed there in canoes, spent months cutting the stone by hand, and then floated it home across open ocean. That journey is where the value came from. A stone was worth more if it was hard to get. If people had risked their lives to bring it home. Every stone carried its story with it. Now think about spending money that weighs as much as a car. You don't carry it anywhere. On Yap, when a stone changed hands, it usually didn't move at all. It stayed right where it was. Everyone simply knew who owned it now. Some of these stones still stand on Yap today, outside homes and meeting houses. And some are still handed over in ceremonies, like weddings. The oldest money on the island still works.
